sectionTitle: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only) (HT only)
topic: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid

specStatements.text: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in the conductor. This is called the generator effect.
An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the size of the induced potential difference/induced current.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the direction of the induced potential difference/induced current.
Students should be able to apply the principles of the generator effect in a given context.
The generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc.
Students should be able to:
• explain how the generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc
• draw/interpret graphs of potential difference generated in the coil against time.
Microphones use the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits.
Students should be able to explain how a moving-coil microphone works.
A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.
Iron is used as it is easily magnetised.
Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents in the core is not required.
The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer Vp and Vs depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns.
potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V
In a step-up transformer Vs > Vp
In a step-down transformer Vs < Vp
If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input.
V_s × I_s = V_p × I_p
Where Vs × Is is the power output (secondary coil) and Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil).
power input and output, in watts, W
Students should be able to:
• explain how the effect of an alternating current in one coil in inducing a current in another is used in transformers
• explain how the ratio of the potential differences across the two coils depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each
• calculate the current drawn from the input supply to provide a particular power output

• apply the equation linking the p.d.s and number of turns in the two coils of a transformer to the currents and the power transfer involved, and relate these to the advantages of power transmission at high potential differences.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents in the core is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The iron core is treated only as the specification treats it: a piece of iron, used because iron is easily magnetised, whose job is to carry the changing magnetic field from the primary coil to the secondary coil. No concept, misconception, stem, option or rationale in this section mentions laminations, eddy currents, hysteresis or any other named cause of core loss. Efficiency appears only in the conditional form the specification uses - if a transformer were 100% efficient the power output would equal the power input - and no item asks why a real transformer falls short of that, so no student is rewarded or penalised for knowing about eddy currents. Questions on why iron is chosen are answerable in full by 'iron is easily magnetised', and questions on why an alternating supply is needed are answerable in full by 'the field in the core must keep changing'.

concepts.definition: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in the conductor. This is called the generator effect.

The potential difference that appears across the ends of a conductor because of relative movement between the conductor and a magnetic field, or because of a change in the magnetic field around it. No cell is needed. A current is induced only if the conductor forms part of a complete circuit.

An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field. This is why a force must be applied, and work done, to keep a generator turning or to push a magnet into a coil.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference
concepts.definition: The size of the induced potential difference or induced current is increased by moving the conductor or magnet faster, by using a stronger magnetic field, and by using a coil with more turns. In short, the faster the magnetic field through the coil changes, the larger the induced potential difference.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the direction of the induced potential difference
concepts.definition: The direction of the induced potential difference or induced current is reversed by reversing the direction of the movement, or by reversing the poles of the magnet, that is by reversing the direction of the magnetic field. Changing the speed or the number of turns alters only the size.

A generator that uses the generator effect to produce alternating current. A coil rotates in a magnetic field and is connected to the external circuit through slip rings, so each end of the coil stays joined to the same contact and the induced potential difference reverses every half turn.

A generator that uses the generator effect to produce direct current. A coil rotates in a magnetic field and is connected to the external circuit through a split-ring commutator, so the connections swap every half turn and the output potential difference never reverses.

The two continuous metal rings, one joined to each end of the rotating coil of an alternator, that keep each end of the coil connected to the same brush all the time. Because the connections never swap, the output alternates in direction as the coil turns.

The divided metal ring used in a dynamo. Every half turn each half of the ring meets the other brush, so the connections to the external circuit swap over at the moment the induced potential difference would otherwise reverse. The output therefore stays in one direction.

concepts.term: Potential difference against time graph for a generator
concepts.definition: For an alternator the graph is a wave that rises and falls equally above and below the time axis, reversing every half turn. For a dynamo the graph is a series of humps all on the same side of the axis. Turning the coil faster makes the peaks both taller and closer together.

A device that uses the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits. The pressure variations make a diaphragm vibrate, the diaphragm moves a coil over a magnet, and the movement of the coil in the magnetic field induces a potential difference that varies in step with the sound wave.

A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic field in the core; that changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating potential difference across it. The two coils are not joined electrically.

The core on which the primary and secondary coils of a basic transformer are wound. Iron is used as it is easily magnetised, so it carries the changing magnetic field from the primary coil through to the secondary coil.

The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer Vp and Vs depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns: Vp / Vs = np / ns, with potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V.

A transformer with more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, so that in a step-up transformer Vs > Vp. Because the power output cannot exceed the power input, the secondary current is smaller than the primary current.

A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, so that in a step-down transformer Vs < Vp. Because the power output cannot exceed the power input, the secondary current is larger than the primary current.

If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input: Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, where Vs × Is is the power output (secondary coil) and Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil), with power input and output, in watts, W.

The unit of potential difference. In the transformer equation the potential difference, Vp and Vs, is in volts, V. A transformer changes the size of a potential difference; it does not change the unit it is measured in.
The unit of power. In the transformer power equation the power input and output, in watts, W, are each found by multiplying a potential difference in volts by a current in amperes.

Power is transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference. For a given power transfer, Vp × Ip is fixed, so raising the potential difference lowers the current in the transmission cables. A smaller current wastes less energy heating the cables, which is the advantage of power transmission at high potential differences.

misconceptions.question: A coil is connected to a sensitive ammeter and there is no cell in the circuit. Can a current flow?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Moving a magnet near the coil induces a potential difference across the coil, and because the circuit is complete a current is induced.
misconceptions.misconception: There can be no current, because every circuit needs a cell or battery to drive one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every circuit a student has built before this topic contains a cell, and 'the cell pushes the charge round' has been the working rule for years. Nothing in that rule prepares them for a source of potential difference that is a piece of moving metal.
misconceptions.correction: The generator effect is itself a source of potential difference. Relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field, or a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, induces a potential difference across the ends of the conductor, with no cell needed.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is pushed into a coil and then held completely still inside it. What does the ammeter read while the magnet is still?
misconceptions.correct: Zero. Nothing is changing, so no potential difference is induced and no current flows.
misconceptions.misconception: A steady current keeps flowing, because the magnet's field is still passing through the coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student pictures the magnetic field itself as the cause, so as long as the magnet is there the effect should continue. The word 'change' in the specification statement is skimmed over.
misconceptions.correction: The generator effect needs relative movement or a change in the magnetic field. A stationary magnet gives a steady field through the coil, nothing is changing, so no potential difference is induced.

misconceptions.question: A north pole is pushed towards a coil. What does the magnetic field of the induced current do to the magnet?
misconceptions.correct: It opposes the change, so the coil end facing the magnet becomes a north pole and repels it.
misconceptions.misconception: The induced field helps the change along, pulling the magnet in faster once it starts moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect effects to reinforce each other, and 'the coil becomes an electromagnet that attracts the magnet' feels natural. The idea of an effect that fights its own cause is unfamiliar.
misconceptions.correction: An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field. If it reinforced the change, energy would appear from nowhere.

misconceptions.question: Why does a bicycle with its dynamo switched on feel harder to pedal?
misconceptions.correct: The induced current makes a magnetic field that opposes the rotation, so more work must be done to keep the coil turning.
misconceptions.misconception: It only feels harder because of ordinary friction in the dynamo's bearings and gears.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Friction is the student's default explanation for anything that resists motion, and the magnetic opposition is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: The opposing force is magnetic, not frictional. Because the induced current's field opposes the change, work must be done against it, and that work is what becomes the electrical energy delivered by the generator.

misconceptions.question: Which change makes the potential difference induced in a coil larger?
misconceptions.correct: Moving the magnet faster, using a stronger magnet, or using a coil with more turns.
misconceptions.misconception: Using thicker or lower-resistance wire for the coil, because that lets more current through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resistance has dominated every electricity topic so far, so the student reaches for it as the controlling factor here too.
misconceptions.correction: The induced potential difference depends on how fast the magnetic field through the coil changes and on the number of turns. The wire's resistance affects the current only after a potential difference has been induced.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is pushed into a coil more quickly than before. What happens to the induced current?
misconceptions.correct: It gets larger, but it is still in the same direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Speeding the magnet up reverses the current, because the factors that change the size also change the direction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The size factors and the direction factors are learned as one undifferentiated list, so any change is assumed to change everything.
misconceptions.correction: Speed, field strength and the number of turns change only the size. Only reversing the direction of the movement or reversing the poles of the magnet reverses the direction.

misconceptions.question: A south pole is pushed into a coil instead of a north pole, at the same speed. What happens to the induced current?
misconceptions.correct: It is the same size but flows in the opposite direction.
misconceptions.misconception: It is exactly the same as before, because the magnet is still moving inwards at the same speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student attends to the motion and ignores the direction of the magnetic field, treating a magnet as a single object rather than as a field with a direction.
misconceptions.correction: Reversing the poles reverses the direction of the magnetic field through the coil, so the induced potential difference and induced current reverse as well.

misconceptions.question: Which generator produces alternating current, an alternator or a dynamo?
misconceptions.correct: The alternator generates ac; the dynamo generates dc.
misconceptions.misconception: The dynamo generates ac and the alternator generates dc.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pair is memorised as a bare fact with no reason attached, so it is easy to swap. Bicycle dynamos are also often ac in real life, which muddies the memory further.
misconceptions.correction: The name is the clue and the hardware is the reason: an alternator has slip rings and alternates, while a dynamo has a split-ring commutator that swaps the connections every half turn so the output stays in one direction.

misconceptions.question: What does the potential difference against time graph of a dynamo look like?
misconceptions.correct: A series of humps, all on the same side of the time axis, rising and falling as the coil turns.
misconceptions.misconception: A flat horizontal line, because a dynamo produces direct current like a cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Direct current' has always been illustrated with the steady output of a cell, so students equate dc with constant.
misconceptions.correction: Direct current means the direction never reverses; it does not mean the size is constant. A dynamo's output rises and falls as the coil turns but never crosses the time axis.

misconceptions.question: Which part gives a dynamo its direct current output?
misconceptions.correct: A split-ring commutator, which swaps the coil's connections to the circuit every half turn.
misconceptions.misconception: A pair of slip rings, which keep each end of the coil joined to the same contact.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Slip rings and commutators look similar in diagrams, and the student remembers that a generator has rings without recording which kind does what.
misconceptions.correction: Slip rings keep the connections fixed, so the output alternates: that is the alternator. The split ring swaps the connections every half turn, so the output stays one way: that is the dynamo.

misconceptions.question: An alternator's coil is turned twice as fast. How does its output graph change?
misconceptions.correct: The peaks become taller and they come twice as often.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the spacing changes; the peaks stay exactly as tall as before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student transfers the idea of frequency from wave topics, where changing frequency need not change amplitude, and forgets that here the speed of rotation also sets how fast the field through the coil changes.
misconceptions.correction: Turning the coil faster makes the magnetic field through it change faster, so the induced potential difference is larger as well as more frequent. Both the height and the spacing of the peaks change.

misconceptions.question: Does a microphone use the generator effect or the motor effect?
misconceptions.correct: The generator effect: movement of a coil in a magnetic field induces a varying current.
misconceptions.misconception: The motor effect, because a current in the coil makes the diaphragm move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Microphones and loudspeakers are built from the same parts and are taught together, so their two directions of energy transfer get exchanged.
misconceptions.correction: A loudspeaker uses the motor effect, turning a varying current into movement and sound. A microphone works the other way, using the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current.

misconceptions.question: In a moving-coil microphone, what actually moves when a sound wave arrives?
misconceptions.correct: The diaphragm and the coil attached to it vibrate; the magnet stays still.
misconceptions.misconception: The sound makes the magnet vibrate inside a coil that is fixed in place.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In classroom demonstrations of induction it is always the magnet that is pushed into the coil, so that picture is carried across even though the device is named after its moving coil.
misconceptions.correction: In a moving-coil microphone the pressure variations move the diaphragm and the coil fixed to it. The coil moves relative to the magnet's field, which is what induces the varying potential difference.

misconceptions.question: How does energy get from the primary coil of a transformer to the secondary coil?
misconceptions.correct: The alternating current in the primary makes a changing magnetic field in the iron core, and that changing field induces a potential difference in the secondary.
misconceptions.misconception: The current itself flows through the iron core, or along a wire joining the two coils.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The core is drawn as a solid metal loop connecting the coils, which looks exactly like a conducting path in a circuit diagram.
misconceptions.correction: The two coils are not joined electrically. The core carries a changing magnetic field, not a current, and it is that changing field through the secondary coil that induces a potential difference.

misconceptions.question: Why is the core of a transformer made of iron?
misconceptions.correct: Iron is used as it is easily magnetised.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron is used because it conducts electricity better than the other metals available.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metal in a circuit diagram means conductor to most students, and iron's magnetic behaviour is not the property they reach for first.
misconceptions.correction: The core's job is magnetic, not electrical. Iron is easily magnetised, so the changing field made by the primary coil is carried strongly through to the secondary coil.

misconceptions.question: A transformer has more turns on the secondary than on the primary. Is the secondary potential difference bigger or smaller?
misconceptions.correct: Bigger, because Vp / Vs = np / ns, so more turns on a coil means a larger potential difference across it.
misconceptions.misconception: Smaller, because the potential difference is shared out between more turns of wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ratio is remembered as a formula with no physical anchor and is written upside down, and the idea of a fixed amount being 'shared out' is borrowed from series circuits.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation exactly as the specification gives it: Vp / Vs = np / ns. More turns on the secondary makes Vs larger than Vp, which is a step-up transformer.

misconceptions.question: Does a step-up transformer increase the power delivered?
misconceptions.correct: No. If the transformer were 100% efficient, the power output would equal the power input.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, stepping up the potential difference steps up the power as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step up' sounds like a general increase, and students rarely separate potential difference from power.
misconceptions.correction: A transformer changes the potential difference and the current together. Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, so a larger secondary potential difference goes with a smaller secondary current, and no extra power is created.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the current when a step-up transformer raises the potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: The current in the secondary coil is smaller than the current in the primary coil.
misconceptions.misconception: The current goes up as well, since a bigger potential difference always pushes a bigger current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: V = I R is applied without noticing that the two coils are separate circuits, so 'more volts means more amps' is carried straight across.
misconceptions.correction: For a 100% efficient transformer Vs × Is = Vp × Ip. If Vs is ten times Vp then Is must be a tenth of Ip, so stepping the potential difference up steps the current down.

misconceptions.question: Would a transformer work if its primary coil were connected to a battery?
misconceptions.correct: No. A steady direct current gives a steady magnetic field, so nothing is induced in the secondary coil.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, it would work in just the same way, because a battery still drives a current through the primary.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student sees the primary current as the thing that matters and does not notice that it is the change in the field, not the field itself, that induces a potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: Only a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference. An alternating current in the primary coil keeps the field in the core changing, which is why transformers need an alternating supply.

misconceptions.question: Why does transmitting power at a high potential difference reduce the energy wasted in the cables?
misconceptions.correct: For a given power, a higher potential difference means a smaller current, and a smaller current heats the cables less.
misconceptions.misconception: A high potential difference lowers the resistance of the transmission cables.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any explanation involving wasted heat is attached to resistance, and students assume the applied potential difference can change it.
misconceptions.correction: The cables' resistance is fixed by what they are made of and how long they are. The high potential difference works by cutting the current, and the heating effect depends on the current in the cables.

misconceptions.question: Does a high transmission potential difference mean a high current in the cables?
misconceptions.correct: No. For a fixed power transfer, raising the potential difference lowers the current.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, a high potential difference pushes a large current along the cables, which is how so much power is delivered.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'High voltage' and 'high current' are treated as the same idea of a powerful supply, and the fixed product V × I is not brought to mind.
misconceptions.correction: Power equals potential difference multiplied by current. If the power transferred is fixed, the two quantities trade off: a very high potential difference goes with a very small current.

misconceptions.question: In the transformer equations, what units are the potential differences and the powers measured in?
misconceptions.correct: Potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V; power input and output, in watts, W.
misconceptions.misconception: The potential differences are in watts and the powers are in volts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol V is used both for the quantity potential difference and for the unit volt, and the letter W is read as a word beginning 'watt' or 'work', so the pairs get crossed.
misconceptions.correction: Potential difference is always measured in volts, V, and power is always measured in watts, W. Multiplying volts by amperes gives watts.

misconceptions.question: In Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, does the equation mean the two currents are equal?
misconceptions.correct: No. It means the two products are equal, so the currents differ whenever the potential differences differ.
misconceptions.misconception: The current in the secondary must equal the current in the primary, because current is conserved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of current in a series circuit is a firmly held rule, and the two coils are wrongly pictured as one circuit.
misconceptions.correction: The coils form two separate circuits. What is shared is the power: Vs × Is is the power output and Vp × Ip is the power input, and only these products are equal.

misconceptions.question: Does adding more turns to a coil change the potential difference induced in it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. More turns on the coil gives a larger induced potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of turns makes no difference, since the magnet and its field have not changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student focuses entirely on the magnet as the active object and treats the coil as a passive piece of wire.
misconceptions.correction: The number of turns is one of the factors that affect the size of the induced potential difference, along with the speed of the relative movement and the strength of the magnetic field.

misconceptions.question: A wire is moved through a magnetic field with its ends not connected to anything. Is anything induced?
misconceptions.correct: A potential difference is induced across the ends of the wire, but no current flows because the circuit is not complete.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing at all is induced, because without a complete circuit there is nothing for the effect to act on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Potential difference and current are not held apart as separate ideas, so removing one is taken to remove the other.
misconceptions.correction: Relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field induces a potential difference across the ends of the conductor whatever it is connected to. A current is induced only if the conductor is part of a complete circuit.

mcqs.stem: A straight copper rod lies horizontally between the poles of a strong magnet. Which action induces a potential difference across the ends of the rod?

options.text: Moving the rod steadily downwards through the magnetic field
options.rationale: The conductor moves relative to the magnetic field, so a potential difference is induced across the ends of the rod.

options.text: Holding the rod still between the poles of a strong magnet
options.rationale: Treats the presence of a magnetic field, rather than a change in it, as the cause of the induced potential difference.

options.text: Joining the ends of the rod with a length of copper wire
options.rationale: Completing a circuit allows a current once a potential difference exists, but by itself it induces nothing.

options.text: Warming the rod so that its resistance rises a little
options.rationale: Resistance affects the current a potential difference can drive; it does not induce a potential difference.

mcqs.stem: A wire is moved through a magnetic field. The two ends of the wire are not connected to anything at all. What is induced in the wire?

options.text: Nothing at all, because the circuit around it is incomplete
options.rationale: Assumes that with no complete circuit there is nothing to induce, merging potential difference with current.

options.text: A current, but no potential difference across the ends
options.rationale: Imagines a current that needs no driving potential difference, in a circuit that is not even complete.

options.text: A potential difference, but no current flows in the wire
options.rationale: A potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor; a current is induced only if the conductor is part of a complete circuit.

options.text: Both a potential difference and a current in the wire
options.rationale: Ignores the condition that the conductor must form part of a complete circuit before a current is induced.

mcqs.stem: The north pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil that is part of a complete circuit. What does the magnetic field produced by the induced current do?

options.text: It reinforces the change, pulling the magnet deeper into the coil
options.rationale: Expects the induced effect to help its own cause, which would create energy from nothing.

options.text: It opposes the change, so it acts to repel the approaching pole
options.rationale: An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, here the movement of the magnet towards the coil.

options.text: It cancels the magnet's own field inside the coil at every instant
options.rationale: Overstates the opposition: the induced field opposes the change, it does not wipe out the magnet's field.

options.text: It acts only on the coil itself and never on the magnet
options.rationale: Denies the interaction that makes a generator harder to turn when it delivers a current.

mcqs.stem: A student pushes a magnet into a coil that is part of a complete circuit. Why must the student do work to keep the magnet moving inwards?

options.text: The induced magnetic field attracts the magnet, so it must be held back
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the opposition backwards; an attracting field would do the work for free.

options.text: Friction in the coil's windings resists the magnet as it moves in
options.rationale: Substitutes ordinary friction for the magnetic opposition that is the reason work must be done.

options.text: The copper wire has resistance, so pushing charge along it takes force
options.rationale: Confuses resistance in the circuit with the force needed to move the magnet.

options.text: An induced magnetic field pushes back on the moving magnet
options.rationale: The induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the movement of the magnet, so a force is needed to keep it moving.

mcqs.stem: A coil is rotated between the poles of a magnet. Which change would increase the size of the potential difference induced in the coil?

options.text: Using thicker copper wire of lower resistance for the coil
options.rationale: Treats resistance as the controlling factor, as it is in earlier electricity topics.

options.text: Winding more turns onto the coil and then rotating it faster
options.rationale: More turns and a faster rate of change of the magnetic field both increase the size of the induced potential difference.

options.text: Holding the coil still in the strongest part of the field
options.rationale: A strong but unchanging field induces nothing, however strong it is.

options.text: Rotating a coil that has far fewer turns of wire on it
options.rationale: Assumes the number of turns is irrelevant, so reducing it is thought to be harmless.

mcqs.stem: A north pole is pushed into a coil and the meter needle flicks to the right. Which change would make the needle flick to the left instead?

options.text: Pushing the same north pole in far more quickly than before
options.rationale: Speed changes only the size of the induced current, never its direction.

options.text: Winding many more turns of wire onto the same coil
options.rationale: The number of turns is a size factor, and is confused here with a direction factor.

options.text: Pushing a much stronger north pole in at the same speed
options.rationale: A stronger magnet gives a bigger flick in the same direction; only reversing the poles reverses it.

options.text: Pulling the same north pole straight back out of the coil
options.rationale: Reversing the direction of the relative movement reverses the direction of the induced potential difference and current.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to an ammeter, held completely still inside the coil for two seconds, and then pulled out. What does the ammeter read while the magnet is held still?

options.text: Zero, because the field through the coil is not changing
options.rationale: With no relative movement and no change in the magnetic field, nothing is induced.

options.text: A steady current, because the magnet's field is inside the coil
options.rationale: Treats the presence of the field, rather than a change in it, as the source of the current.

options.text: A current in the opposite direction to the one during the push
options.rationale: Invents a reversal where there is no change in the field at all.

options.text: A current that grows slowly while the magnet is inside
options.rationale: Imagines the effect building up over time, again treating the field itself as the cause.

mcqs.stem: A wire is moved downwards between the poles of a magnet, and then moved upwards at twice the speed. Compared with the downward movement, the potential difference induced during the upward movement is:

options.text: twice the size, in the same direction as before
options.rationale: Gets the size right but ignores that reversing the movement reverses the direction.

options.text: the same size, but in the opposite direction
options.rationale: Gets the direction right but overlooks the doubled speed, which doubles the size.

options.text: twice the size, in the opposite direction
options.rationale: Doubling the speed doubles the size, and reversing the direction of movement reverses the direction of the induced potential difference.

options.text: half the size, in the same direction as it was
options.rationale: Inverts the effect of speed and misses the reversal as well.

mcqs.stem: An alternator and a dynamo are both turned steadily by the same motor. How do their outputs differ?

options.text: The dynamo generates ac and the alternator generates dc
options.rationale: Swaps the two devices, a pair often memorised without any reason attached.

options.text: Both generate ac, though the dynamo's output is larger
options.rationale: Ignores the split-ring commutator that keeps the dynamo's output in one direction.

options.text: The alternator generates ac, while the dynamo generates dc
options.rationale: The generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc.

options.text: The alternator uses the motor effect, not induction
options.rationale: Confuses the motor effect with the generator effect, which both generators use.

mcqs.stem: A dynamo and an alternator have identical coils and magnets. Which part of the dynamo makes its output a direct current?

options.text: A split-ring commutator, which swaps the connections every half turn
options.rationale: Swapping the connections each half turn keeps the output potential difference in one direction.

options.text: A pair of slip rings, which keep the coil joined to the same contacts
options.rationale: Slip rings are the alternator's hardware, and they let the output alternate.

options.text: A commutator that holds the output at one steady value
options.rationale: Assumes direct current must be constant, so the commutator is thought to smooth it.

options.text: An iron core that stores the current between the half turns
options.rationale: Treats the iron core as something that carries or stores current rather than magnetic field.

mcqs.stem: Which describes the graph of potential difference generated in the coil against time for a dynamo turning steadily?

options.text: A straight horizontal line at one constant positive value
options.rationale: Equates direct current with a constant output, as from a cell.

options.text: A wave that rises and falls equally either side of the axis
options.rationale: This is the alternator's graph; the dynamo's output does not reverse.

options.text: A line rising steadily as the coil keeps turning
options.rationale: Imagines the output accumulating with each turn rather than following the coil's rotation.

options.text: A series of humps that never cross below the time axis
options.rationale: The dynamo's output rises and falls as the coil turns but never reverses direction.

mcqs.stem: The coil of an alternator is turned twice as fast as before. How does the graph of potential difference against time change?

options.text: The peaks are taller but just as far apart
options.rationale: Notices the larger potential difference but not the higher frequency.

options.text: The peaks are taller and closer together
options.rationale: A faster rotation changes the field through the coil faster, giving a larger induced potential difference more often.

options.text: The peaks are closer but no taller than before
options.rationale: Transfers the wave idea that frequency can change without amplitude changing.

options.text: The peaks are lower and further apart than before
options.rationale: Reverses both effects of turning the coil faster.

mcqs.stem: How does a microphone make use of the generator effect?

options.text: Variations in current are converted into pressure variations in the air
options.rationale: Describes a loudspeaker, which uses the motor effect, not a microphone.

options.text: Sound waves alter the resistance of the coil, so the current varies
options.rationale: Invokes a change of resistance instead of an induced potential difference.

options.text: Sound waves are absorbed by a magnet, which then makes a current
options.rationale: Leaves out the relative movement between coil and magnet that induces the potential difference.

options.text: Pressure variations in a sound wave are converted into variations in current
options.rationale: Microphones use the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave reaches the diaphragm of a moving-coil microphone. What happens next?

options.text: The diaphragm makes the magnet vibrate inside a coil that is fixed
options.rationale: Borrows the classroom demonstration where the magnet is the moving part.

options.text: The diaphragm and its coil vibrate near a magnet, inducing a current
options.rationale: The coil moving in the magnetic field induces a potential difference that varies in step with the pressure variations.

options.text: A current in the coil makes the diaphragm vibrate and give out a sound
options.rationale: Runs the energy transfer backwards, describing a loudspeaker.

options.text: The diaphragm presses on a crystal, which is magnetised by sound
options.rationale: Replaces induction with an invented mechanism that involves no relative movement in a field.

mcqs.stem: What does a basic transformer consist of?

options.text: A primary coil and a secondary coil joined by a copper wire
options.rationale: Adds an electrical connection between coils that are in fact linked only magnetically.

options.text: Two coils wound on a plastic former that fully insulates them
options.rationale: Chooses the core material for its electrical properties instead of its magnetic ones.

options.text: A primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core
options.rationale: This is exactly the construction given in the specification.

options.text: One coil on an iron core fitted with a sliding contact
options.rationale: Describes a variable resistor arrangement rather than a transformer's two separate coils.

mcqs.stem: Why is the core of a basic transformer made of iron?

options.text: Iron is easily magnetised by the changing field
options.rationale: Iron is used as it is easily magnetised, so it carries the changing field to the secondary coil.

options.text: Iron conducts an electric current better than copper
options.rationale: Picks an electrical property, and one that is not even true of iron.

options.text: Iron carries the current across from one coil to the other
options.rationale: Treats the core as a conducting path between coils that are not joined electrically.

options.text: Iron does not get hot when a current flows in it
options.rationale: Again treats the core as part of the electrical circuit rather than the magnetic path.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly links the potential differences and the numbers of turns on the two coils of a transformer?

options.text: Vp / Vs = np / ns, so the ratio of the pds equals the ratio of the turns
options.rationale: This is the equation as the specification states it, with potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V.

options.text: Vp / Vs = ns / np, so the ratio of the pds is the inverse turns ratio
options.rationale: Writes the ratio upside down, so a step-up transformer would be read as a step-down one.

options.text: Vp + Vs = np + ns, so the pds and the turns must add up to match
options.rationale: Replaces the ratio with a sum, treating the potential difference as shared out.

options.text: Vp × Ip = np / ns, which links the input power to the turns
options.rationale: Mixes the power equation with the turns-ratio equation.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 40 turns on its primary coil and 800 turns on its secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary coil is 15 V. What is the potential difference across the secondary coil?

options.rationale: Uses the turns ratio upside down: 15 × 40 / 800, giving a step-down result.
Multiplies 15 by 800 and forgets to divide by the 40 turns on the primary.
Gives the turns ratio itself, 800 / 40, instead of using it on the primary potential difference.
Vp / Vs = np / ns, so Vs = 15 × 800 / 40 = 300 V, a step-up transformer with Vs > Vp.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 1200 turns on its primary coil, 60 turns on its secondary coil, and a primary potential difference of 240 V. Which describes this transformer and its secondary potential difference?

options.text: Step-up, and the secondary potential difference becomes 4800 V
options.rationale: Inverts the turns ratio, turning a step-down transformer into a step-up one.

options.text: Step-down, but the secondary pd is only about 180 V
options.rationale: Subtracts, taking 60 from 240, instead of using the ratio of the numbers of turns.

options.text: Step-down, and the secondary potential difference is 12 V
options.rationale: Fewer turns on the secondary gives Vs < Vp: Vs = 240 × 60 / 1200 = 12 V.

options.text: Step-up, so the secondary current is 20 times larger
options.rationale: Reads more turns on the primary as stepping up, and raises the current alongside.

mcqs.stem: Which units belong with the quantities in the transformer equations?

options.text: Potential difference in watts, W; and power in volts, V
options.rationale: Swaps the two units, a slip encouraged by the symbols V and W.

options.text: Potential difference in volts, V; power in watts, W
options.rationale: Potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V; power input and output, in watts, W.

options.text: Potential difference in volts, V; power in amperes, A
options.rationale: Gives the unit of current for power, confusing the factors with the product.

options.text: Potential difference in amperes, A; power in joules, J
options.rationale: Uses the unit of energy for power and the unit of current for potential difference.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is described as 100% efficient. What does this tell you about its coils?

options.text: The current in the secondary coil equals the current in the primary coil
options.rationale: Reads Vs × Is = Vp × Ip as though the currents themselves were equal.

options.text: The secondary coil delivers more power than the primary takes in
options.rationale: Treats a transformer as a source of extra power rather than a device that trades pd against current.

options.text: The power output at the secondary equals the power input at the primary
options.rationale: If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input: Vs × Is = Vp × Ip.

options.text: No current at all is drawn by the primary coil from the supply
options.rationale: Confuses perfect efficiency with drawing nothing from the supply.

mcqs.stem: A transformer that can be treated as 100% efficient supplies 24 W to a lamp from a 230 V mains supply. What current is drawn from the input supply?

options.rationale: Multiplies 230 by 24 instead of dividing the power by the potential difference.
Vp × Ip equals the power output, so Ip = 24 / 230 = 0.104 A.
Divides the wrong way round, 230 / 24, giving a current far too large for a 24 W lamp.
Reads the power in watts straight off as a current in amperes.

mcqs.stem: Why is electrical power transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference?

options.text: A high pd means a small current, so less energy heats the cables
options.rationale: For a fixed power transfer Vp × Ip is fixed, so a higher potential difference gives a smaller current and less heating of the cables.

options.text: A high pd lowers the resistance of the cables, so less energy is wasted
options.rationale: Attaches the saving to a change in resistance, which the applied potential difference cannot alter.

options.text: A high pd drives a large current, which carries the power to homes faster
options.rationale: Treats high potential difference and high current as the same idea of a powerful supply.

options.text: A high pd increases the power delivered to each of the homes
options.rationale: Confuses the potential difference used for transmission with the power a home receives.

mcqs.stem: Why must the supply connected to the primary coil of a transformer be an alternating current?

options.text: A direct current cannot pass along the wire of the primary coil at all
options.rationale: Invents an electrical block; a direct current flows perfectly well in the primary.

options.text: An alternating current can jump the gap between the two coils
options.rationale: Imagines charge crossing from one coil to the other rather than a magnetic field linking them.

options.text: A direct current would make the iron core melt with the heat
options.rationale: Offers a damage story in place of the requirement for a changing magnetic field.

options.text: Only a changing current gives a changing field in the core
options.rationale: An alternating current keeps the magnetic field in the core changing, and only a changing field induces a potential difference in the secondary coil.
